section_1.title: Prerequisites: Vectors in 3D Space
section_1.content: Briefly define vectors as directed segments in 3D space. Introduce the concept of a 'parallelogram' spanned by two vectors, u and v, as the geometric foundation for the cross product.
section_1.example: Imagine two robotic arms positioned at the origin, pointing in different directions; the space between them represents the 'tent' or parallelogram we aim to measure.

section_2.title: Definition of the Cross Product
section_2.content: Introduce the cross product result as a vector perpendicular to the original plane. Use the Right-Hand Rule to determine the direction. Emphasize that the magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by the two input vectors.
section_2.example: A spinning propeller blade: the vectors follow the blade, while the cross-product vector points straight out along the axle, indicating the axis of rotation.

section_3.title: Geometric Intuition & Determinants
section_3.content: Visualize the cross product as a determinant calculation. Explain that if the area (determinant) is zero, the vectors are collinear (overlapping). This provides a intuitive measure of 'how parallel' or 'how independent' vectors are.
section_3.example: A digital artist using a 3D modeling tool: dragging two vectors—if they are perfectly aligned, the cross product vanishes, signaling the 'collapse' of the 3D surface area.

section_4.title: Linear Transformations and Orientation
section_4.content: Explain the cross product as a linear transformation where the input vectors are mapped to a new space. Discuss how the cross product preserves (or flips) the orientation (handedness) of the coordinate system.
section_4.example: A character in a video game moving through a portal: the cross product helps calculate the surface normal, ensuring the character walks on the ground rather than falling through the wall.

section_5.title: Summary & Application
section_5.content: Recap: Cross product = Perpendicular vector + Area calculation. Connect this to real-world physics, such as torque (force x lever arm) which is the classic application of this geometric relationship.
section_5.example: An animation of a wrench tightening a bolt: the 'force' vector and 'lever arm' vector combine via cross product to show the resulting torque vector moving the bolt forward.
